entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
Bec Abbey (Abbaye Notre-Dame du Bec) in Normandy, France, founded c. 1034 by the knight Herluin who renounced his military career for monastic life, became in the 11th-12th centuries the most intellectually influential monastery in Western Christendom — not because of its wealth or political power, but because of the extraordinary scholars it attracted. Lanfranc of Pavia (prior 1045-1063), the Italian-born teacher who made Bec famous for its school, was followed by Anselm of Aosta (prior 1063-1078) — one of the greatest philosophers of the Middle Ages, whose Proslogion (1077-78) contained the ontological argument for God's existence.

Anselm's impact through Bec was enormous: he became Archbishop of Canterbury (1093-1109) and his philosophical works — the Cur Deus Homo (Why God Became Man), the Monologion, and Proslogion — defined the 'faith seeking understanding' approach that shaped Scholastic theology for centuries. Lanfranc also became Archbishop of Canterbury (1070-1089), reorganizing the English church after the Norman Conquest. Bec thus supplied two of the most consequential Archbishops of Canterbury in English church history through its intellectual tradition.

Bec Abbey was suppressed during the French Revolution (1790), its buildings sold and converted to a prison. The community was restored in 1948 and the abbey continues as a Benedictine monastery today. Its medieval library — which once held manuscripts studied by Anselm — was dispersed, but the intellectual tradition it created in the 11th century shaped Western theology and philosophy for the subsequent millennium.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Bec Abbey — producing Anselm's ontological argument (the most debated proof for God's existence in Western philosophy), supplying two of Canterbury's most consequential archbishops, and establishing Scholasticism's foundational method — was the 11th century's most intellectually influential institution in Western Christendom.
